native_notes.13:10: Hebrew michyat basar chai literally means "a reviving patch of living flesh," referring to exposed raw flesh; michyah (from chayah, "to live/revive") likewise denotes the raw regenerating area of a burn in verse 24.
native_notes.13:30: Hebrew neteq (from the root nataq, "to pull away/pluck") denotes a scaly scalp or beard disorder associated with hair loss, rendered "scall."
native_notes.13:33: Hebrew contrasts the reflexive Hithpael verb hitgallach ("shave himself") with the transitive Piel yegalleach ("shave [the scall]").
native_notes.13:39: Hebrew bohaq occurs only here in the Old Testament and denotes a harmless, pale skin eruption distinct from ritual leprosy.
native_notes.13:51: Hebrew mam'eret (Hiphil participle of ma'ar) literally means "causing pain" or "eating away," denoting an active, destructive affliction in fabric, leather, or walls (cf. 14:44).
native_notes.13:55: Hebrew hukkabbes is a rare Hothpaal infinitive construct ("after being washed"); the verse also reuses qarachatto and gabbachto ("its bald back or bald front," cf. vv. 42-43) metaphorically for the worn underside or topside of the fabric.
native_notes.14:3: Hebrew tsara'at, rendered "leprosy" here, covers a range of ritually defiling skin disorders as well as discoloring or moldlike conditions on garments and plastered walls (vv. 34, 55), not solely modern Hansen's disease. "Healed in the leprous person" translates a pregnant Hebrew construction (literally "healed from the leprous person," i.e., healed away from him), using the Qal passive participle tsaru'a alongside the Pual participle metsora' in v. 2.
native_notes.14:10: Hebrew issaron ("tenth-measure") is one-tenth of an ephah (a dry measure of roughly 2.2 liters), and a log is a small liquid measure equal to one-twelfth of a hin (roughly one-third of a liter).
native_notes.14:21: "His means are insufficient" renders the Hebrew idiom 'en yado masseget (literally "his hand does not reach," Hiphil participle of nasag), which recurs in vv. 22, 30, 31, and 32 to express financial ability.
native_notes.14:37: "Sunken patches" translates the hapax legomenon sheqa'arurot (apparently from shaqa', "to sink"), and "lower than the wall" renders shaphal min-haqqir, meaning recessed beneath the wall surface.
native_notes.14:49: "To purify" renders the privative Piel infinitive lechatte' (from chata', "to sin," here meaning "to purge from defilement," also in v. 52), distinct from the Piel of taher ("to cleanse" or "declare clean," vv. 7, 11, 48).
native_notes.15:2: Hebrew basar ("flesh") is used here and in vv. 3 and 19 as a euphemism for the genital organ.
native_notes.15:3: Hebrew rar (Qal perfect of the hapax legomenon verb rir, "ooze" or "run") and hechtim (Hiphil perfect of chatam, "seal up" or "obstruct") cover both a continuous discharge and a blocked one.
native_notes.15:13: Hebrew mayim chayyim ("living water") is the standard idiom for fresh, flowing water from a spring or stream.
native_notes.15:23: The masculine pronoun hu ("it") has no explicit antecedent and is widely understood to refer to any object lying on the bed or article on which the menstruating woman sits.
native_notes.15:31: The verb vehizzartem is the Hiphil of nazar ("set apart" or "keep separate"); some ancient versions reflect a form of zahar ("warn").
native_notes.16:2: Hebrew hakkapporet ("atonement cover") is derived from the root kafar ("cover" or "atone").
native_notes.16:8: The meaning of Hebrew Azazel is uncertain; it has been understood variously as a wilderness figure or demon, a remote rugged place, or a term signifying complete removal ("the goat that departs").
native_notes.16:21: Hebrew ish itti uses the hapax legomenon adjective itti (from et, "time"), meaning a man ready or designated for the occasion. In addition, yadav ("his hands") is written defectively without yod in the Masoretic Text.
native_notes.16:22: Hebrew erets gezerah (from gazar, "cut off") literally means "a cut-off land," denoting an isolated, uninhabited region.
native_notes.16:32: Literally "whose hand one fills," using the Hebrew idiom mille yad ("fill the hand") for priestly ordination; both yimshach ("anoint") and yemalle ("fill") are indefinite third-person singular active verbs rendered passively.
native_notes.17:7: Hebrew se'irim (plural of sa'ir, literally "hairy ones" or "he-goats") refers to goat-shaped desert demons or deities (cf. 2 Chr 11:15; Isa 13:21).
native_notes.17:9: Hebrew me'ammayw uses the plural noun ("from his kinspeople"), contrasting with the singular noun in "from the midst of his people" in vv. 4 and 10.
native_notes.17:11: The Hebrew noun nephesh ("life" or "person") occurs three times in this verse, linking the life of flesh in blood to human lives; the preposition be- in bannephesh ("by means of the life") is instrumental or denotes equivalence.
native_notes.17:14: Literally, "its blood is in/as its life" (damo venaphsho hu'), an emphatic Hebrew construction combining casus pendens with a beth of equivalence or identity.
native_notes.18:6: The Hebrew pairs the distributive singular phrase "any man ... his flesh" with the second-person plural verb lo' tiqrevu ("you shall not approach"); she'er besaro is literally "flesh of his flesh," an idiom for close blood kin.
native_notes.18:18: The Qal infinitive construct litsror derives from tsarar ("to be a rival wife" or "to create rivalry," cognate with tsarah, "rival wife," in 1 Sam 1:6).
native_notes.18:20: Literally, "you must not give your lying for seed" (lo'-titten shekhavtekha lezara'), an idiom for sexual intercourse; the noun zera' ("seed") also creates a verbal link to "your seed" (mizzar'akha) in v. 21.
native_notes.18:21: The Hiphil infinitive construct leha'avir (literally "to cause to pass over") appears here without the phrase "through the fire" found in parallel texts (e.g., Deut 18:10; 2 Kgs 23:10), denoting dedication or child sacrifice to Molech.
native_notes.18:30: Hebrew uses the same noun huqqot ("statutes") for the nations' "abominable statutes" (cf. v. 3) as for the LORD's "statutes" in vv. 4, 5, and 26, underscoring the deliberate contrast between them.
native_notes.19:5: Hebrew lirsonkem literally means "for your acceptance," referring to cultic acceptability before the LORD (matching the Niphal verb yeraseh, "it will be accepted," in v. 7) rather than mere personal inclination.
native_notes.19:16: Hebrew al-dam re'eka literally means "upon/against the blood of your neighbor," an idiom understood either as taking a stand against a neighbor's life (for instance, through false accusation) or as standing idly by while a neighbor's life is in mortal danger.
native_notes.19:19: The rare Hebrew noun sha'atnez (occurring only here and in Deut 22:11) denotes cloth of mixed weave, explained in Deut 22:11 specifically as wool and linen woven together.
native_notes.19:20: Hebrew biqqoret is a hapax legomenon from the root bqr ("inquire/examine"), denoting a judicial inquiry or assessment, though interpreters have also understood it as a penalty, scourging, or indemnity. Note also the emphatic construction hofdeh lo nifdatah, pairing a Hophal infinitive absolute with a Niphal perfect ("not at all been redeemed").
native_notes.19:23: Hebrew va'araltem orlato et-piryo literally says "you shall treat as uncircumcised its foreskin, namely its fruit," applying the metaphor of uncircumcision to forbid eating a fruit tree's produce during its first three years.
native_notes.20:3: Hebrew zera ("seed") here denotes a person's children/offspring (retaining the verbal link with Lev 18:20–21; cf. 20:2, 4).
native_notes.20:9: Hebrew damav (literally "his bloods," plural) is a standard legal idiom for bloodguilt, here meaning the offender bears sole responsibility for his own execution. The conjunction ve- ("and") in "his father and his mother" carries the legal disjunctive sense "or" (as also in v. 19).
native_notes.20:17: Hebrew hesed here is a rare homonym (hesed II, cf. Prov 14:34) meaning "disgrace" or "reproach," distinct from the common word hesed ("loyal love, kindness").
native_notes.20:25: The Piel infinitive letamme carries a declarative or estimative sense ("to treat/declare as unclean"), while the verse arranges the pairs chiastically: clean-to-unclean for animals, then unclean-to-clean for birds.
native_notes.20:27: Hebrew ki-yihyeh bahem ov o yidde'oni literally means "when there is in them a spirit of the dead or a divining ('knowing') spirit." By metonymy, the same two nouns denote the mediums and spirit-diviners who consult such spirits in 19:31 and 20:6.
native_notes.21:4: Hebrew ba'al be'ammav is syntactically difficult and may mean 'as a leader among his people' or 'as a husband among his people' (referring to a wife or relatives by marriage). The form lehehallo is a Niphal infinitive construct of halal ('profane') with a 3ms suffix, 'so as to profane himself.'
native_notes.21:5: The ketiv is written yqrhh; the qere yiqrechu ('they shall make bald'), translated here, is plural like the following verbs and is followed by the cognate noun qorhah ('a bald spot').
native_notes.21:9: The verb tehel is Niphal imperfect 3fs of halal I ('profane herself'), echoing the Piel participle mehallelet ('she profanes') in the following clause.
native_notes.21:10: Literally 'and one has filled his hand' (Piel perfect of male' with an impersonal subject), the standard priestly idiom for ordination.
native_notes.21:20: Several rare defect terms in vv. 18-20 have uncertain exact meanings: harum (v. 18) likely denotes a cleft or flattened nose or face, saru'a (v. 18) an abnormally long limb, daq (v. 20) someone stunted or a dwarf, and teballul (v. 20) a blurring or spot in the eye.
native_notes.22:2: The Niphal yinnazeru (from nazar) means 'keep themselves separate' or 'abstain.' In the Masoretic clause order, the relative clause 'which they dedicate to Me' follows 'My holy name,' resuming 'the holy things of the sons of Israel.'
native_notes.22:16: The Hiphil weqatal vehissi'u (from nasa', 'cause to bear') has an ambiguous object pronoun 'otam ('them'), referring either to the Israelites (whom negligent priests cause to incur guilt) or reflexively to the offenders themselves; 'avon 'ashmah is a construct chain, literally 'iniquity of guilt.'
native_notes.22:19: Hebrew lirtsonekhem ('for your acceptance,' also in v. 29) indicates that the offering must meet the standard to be accepted on the worshiper's behalf, matching leratson ('for acceptance') in vv. 20-21 and the Niphal of ratsah ('be accepted') in vv. 23, 25, and 27.
native_notes.22:24: The four Qal passive participles (ma'uk, katut, natuq, karut) refer to methods of animal castration or testicular injury; the closing clause ('nor shall you do this in your land') is commonly understood to forbid castrating animals in Israel.
native_notes.23:5: Hebrew beyn ha-arbayim (dual of erev) literally means "between the two evenings," an idiom referring either to twilight between sunset and dusk or to the late afternoon hours before sunset.
native_notes.23:7: Hebrew meleket avodah literally means "work of labor/service," denoting regular occupational work, in contrast to the total prohibition of all melakah ("work") on the Sabbath (v. 3) and the Day of Atonement (vv. 28-31).
native_notes.23:11: Hebrew mimmohorat ha-shabbat ("on the day after the Sabbath") has been interpreted either as the day after the first festival day of Unleavened Bread or as the day after the weekly Sabbath falling during the festival; similarly, "seven complete Sabbaths" in v. 15 denotes seven full weeks culminating in the seventh Sabbath (v. 16).
native_notes.23:13: Hebrew esronim (plural of issaron, "tenth-measure") is a dry measure equal to one-tenth of an ephah; the spelling veniskoh ("and its drink offering") preserves an archaic third-person masculine singular suffix written with he.
native_notes.23:27: Hebrew ve-innitem et-nafshoteikem (Piel of anah II) literally means "humble/afflict your souls," an idiom for fasting and self-denial; the corresponding Pual passive te-unneh ("is humbled") appears in v. 29.
native_notes.24:6: Hebrew ma-arakot (derived from arak, "arrange") denotes ordered rows or stacks of loaves arranged upon the pure table.
native_notes.24:11: Hebrew vayyiqqov (Qal wayyiqtol of naqav) with et-ha-shem ("the Name," referring to the LORD's name, cf. v. 16) means "blasphemed/reviled" here, though naqav can also mean "designate" or "pronounce distinctly."
native_notes.24:12: Hebrew lifrosh (Qal infinitive construct of parash, "make clear/distinct") is used impersonally with al-pi ("by the mouth of") and the divine name to indicate waiting for a clear divine verdict.
native_notes.24:19: Hebrew mum ("injury") is the same term used for a physical defect or blemish in Leviticus 21-22; the active Qal yitten ("inflicts") in vv. 19-20 is mirrored by the passive Niphal yinnaten ("shall be inflicted") of the same verb natan at the end of v. 20.
native_notes.25:5: Hebrew nezirekha (from nazir, "consecrated/untrimmed one") metaphorically designates an unpruned vine whose tendrils grow freely during the Sabbatical year, like a Nazirite's uncut hair (also in v. 11).
native_notes.25:26: The verb "prospers" renders the Hebrew idiom hissigah yado (Hiphil of nasag plus yad, literally "his hand reaches/attains"), denoting the acquisition of sufficient financial means (also in vv. 47 and 49).
native_notes.25:30: Ketiv/Qere: The ketiv (written form) reads lo ("not," i.e., "that does not have a wall"), whereas the qere (read form, translated here) reads lo ("to it," i.e., "that has a wall"), matching the contrast with unwalled villages in vv. 29 and 31.
native_notes.25:33: The Masoretic text reads an active Qal verb ("if one of the Levites redeems") without a negative particle (unlike the Vulgate, which supplies "not"), indicating that even a house redeemed by a fellow Levite reverts at the Jubilee. Literally "the sale of a house and the city of his possession," with the conjunction functioning epexegetically ("in the city of his possession").
native_notes.25:42: Hebrew uses the single noun eved ("servant/slave") both for Israel as the LORD's servants and for chattel slaves (also in v. 55), underscoring that Israel already belongs to the LORD and cannot be permanently enslaved to human masters.
native_notes.26:21: The rare noun rendered 'opposition' occurs in the Hebrew Bible only in Leviticus 26 (vv. 21, 23, 24, 27, 28, 40, 41). Derived from a root meaning 'encounter' or 'run counter to,' it denotes defiant contrariety or hostility, though some ancient interpreters took it as treating God's deeds as mere chance.
native_notes.26:30: The Hebrew noun rendered 'incense altars' was historically associated with the sun, but West Semitic archaeological inscriptions identify the term as an incense altar or brazier.
native_notes.26:34: The verb rendered 'make up for' (Qal) and 'repay' (a rare Hiphil perfect form) reflects the restitution sense of paying off an unpaid debt, linking the land's Sabbaths with Israel paying for its iniquity in vv. 41 and 43; some take the Qal here in the homonymous sense 'enjoy.' The form rendered 'it lies desolate' (also in vv. 35, 43) is a rare Hophal infinitive construct of the root meaning 'be desolate.'
native_notes.26:41: The Hebrew imperfect verb 'walked' expresses the past consequence of Israel's opposition in v. 40, and the compound conjunction 'if then' resumes the conditional clause before the covenant promise in v. 42.
native_notes.26:42: Literally 'My covenant, Jacob' (and similarly with Isaac and Abraham), an unusual Hebrew construction in which a suffixed noun stands directly before a proper name to mean 'My covenant with Jacob.'
native_notes.27:2: Hebrew uses the crystallized Priestly noun erkeka (literally "your assessment") throughout Leviticus 27; its fossilized second-person suffix functions as part of a fixed technical term that even takes the definite article in 27:23 and stands before a following noun in 27:3, 5, 6, and 12.
native_notes.27:8: Literally "according to what the hand of the one making the vow reaches" (Hiphil imperfect of nsg), an established Hebrew idiom for what a person can afford.
native_notes.27:26: The Pual imperfect yebukkar (from bkr, occurring in the Pual only here in the Hebrew Bible) denotes an animal born into or accorded firstborn status as automatically belonging to the LORD.
native_notes.27:28: Hebrew herem and its cognate verbs (Hiphil in 27:28; Hophal in 27:29) denote irrevocable devotion to the LORD, whether permanent, unredeemable consecration to the sanctuary (27:21, 28) or, in judicial and warfare bans, consignment to death (27:29).
